extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in poetics and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for judging, writing, and defending poetry—especially lyric and descriptive poetry—and for conducting fair literary criticism. Emphasises distinctions of faculty (fancy vs imagination), proper critical method, and stylistic ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging genius by accidental failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not decide on the merits of a poet or painter by accidental failures or faulty passages; 'where there is genius, these [defects] always point to his characteristic beauties; but' it is vile to decide by accidental failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not single out minor slips and treat them as representative. Examples: ridiculing marginal technical faults (e.g., background trees rendered poorly) while ignoring the artist’s characteristic achievements. The critic who reprints and amplifies the worst passages (sometimes increasing their circulation ten- or twenty-fold) commits an injustice and a folly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasise and elucidate beauties rather than merely pointing out defects
rubrics_metrics.description: He who points out and elucidates the beauties of an original work gives interesting information; by contrast, he who tells me of defects tells me nothing I should not have taken for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviews should instruct readers by explaining why parts of a work are admirable—this is valuable information that alters a reader’s perception; mere cataloguing of faults is unhelpful. Critics should therefore balance or prioritise exposition of merits over enumeration of failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support reviews by reference to fixed canons deduced from human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be conducted on principles and with motives such that reviewers 'support their decisions by reference to fixed canons of criticism, previously established and deduced from the nature of man.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary dictation and petulant sneers. Critics should derive judgement from consistent aesthetic principles (canons) rather than personal whim, rancour, or temporary fashions; such principled criticism lends authority and fairness to reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent critical standards to living and dead authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed works should not be judged by a different rule merely because the author is alive; 'why should we judge by a different rule two printed works, only because the one author is alive, and the other in his grave?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playful or light compositions by living authors ('haec ipsi novimus esse nihil') should not be condemned differently from similar works by dead authors; maintain uniform standards across authorship status when evaluating moral or artistic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerate harmless trifles and playful compositions if not immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions which would be enjoyed or passed over according to taste—'provided they contained nothing immoral'—should not be censured simply because they are trifling; 'periturae parcere chartae is emphatically an unreasonable demand.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor, playful, or ephemeral pieces can legitimately occupy ink and paper; critics should not treat every printed trifle as a crime against literature so long as it causes no moral harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for authorial intention when evaluating stylistic choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When passages are intentionally written in a humbler or 'colloquial' style (as Wordsworth announced), critics should not treat them as mere imperfections; hostility arose when humbler passages were announced as intentional choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a poet explicitly states that certain effects are deliberate, critics must judge those passages in light of the declared aesthetic aim rather than assuming negligence or incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate genuine simplicity from mere affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'a downright simpleness' that may be a genuine poetic choice and an affected, barren counterfeit of poetry; one must not conflate sincere simplicity with an 'affectation of simplicity' or bald imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should analyse whether plain language and simple forms arise from authentic poetic vision (which can be powerful) or from poor taste or contrivance that deserves censure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow a few inferior pieces to condemn a whole collection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unjust to fix attention on a few separate and insulated poems with as much aversion as if they were 'plague-spots on the whole work' instead of passing them over as blank paper or minor coins in a rouleau of gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate collections holistically: weigh the whole body of work, and treat inferior or trivial pieces as negligible unless they reveal pervasive defects or immorality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fancy from imagination as two different faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy and Imagination are two distinct and widely different faculties, not merely synonyms or degrees of the same power; 'to the faculty by which I had characterized Milton, we should confine the term “imagination;” while the other would be contra-distinguished as “fancy.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and use this distinction in critical theory: attribute higher, formative, and unifying creative powers to 'imagination' and reserve 'fancy' for lower associative or decorative mental operations. This nomenclature influences both critique and poetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagination is the faculty that unites deep feeling with profound thought; it balances truthful observation with the power to modify and idealise, 'the original gift of spreading the tone, the atmosphere, and with it the depth and height of the ideal world around forms, incidents, and situations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imaginative poetry (e.g., Milton, Wordsworth at his best) creates an atmosphere and ideal world that elevates ordinary objects, and requires the critic and poet to recognise its unifying and formative power rather than reducing it to picturesque ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of Fancy and common defects to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: Fancy tends toward crowding of images, arbitrary and illogical phrases, strained diction, and often 'prosaic words in feeble metre, silly thoughts in childish phrases'—the sort of hackneyed or fantastic technique that undermines greatness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets should avoid relying on fancy’s mere assemblage of striking phrases or forced effects; critics should recognise when imagery and diction stem from mere fanciful assemblage rather than from true imaginative synthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius tends to purify itself; early faults are often transient
rubrics_metrics.description: In the poetic development, genius 'clears and purifies itself from the faults and errors of its earliest products'—early obtrusive or heterogeneous elements often serve as ferment that later disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a poet’s early works, allow for development and maturation; early obscurities or contortions may be instructive stages rather than immutable flaws. Example: Wordsworth’s early Descriptive Sketches show knotty style that later subsides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: avoid forced diction and illogical, hackneyed phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic phraseology should not resort to 'arbitrary and illogical phrases, at once hackneyed and fantastic' which will 'alloy' even the earliest true genius unless attention is specially directed to their worthlessness and incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for language that arises naturally from thought and feeling; prefer clarity and organic diction over strained effects. Be mindful that certain stanza forms (e.g., Spenserian) may invite colloquial descent, but such choices must be controlled to avoid obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical humility: recognise uncertainty and avoid quarrelling from discomfort
rubrics_metrics.description: When critics confront perplexity (uncertainty that the author may be right), they are predisposed to anger and may quarrel with the author to alleviate unease—such reaction is a sign of poor critical temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should acknowledge their own uncertainty and resist the impulse to denounce out of discomfort; measured enquiry and openness to revision are marks of sound criticism.
